hints: Scan the seven structures for a carbon bonded to four different groups, remembering that aldehyde and ketone carbonyl carbons cannot be chiral.
Recall how to show a pair of mirror image isomers using solid wedge, dashed wedge and normal lines around the chiral centre.
walkthrough:
Spot the only chiral centre**
Picture each carbon skeleton. You need a carbon with four different attachments. P is straight chain, R has $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}$, S has $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}$, T, U, V are ketones with no such carbon. Only Q, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CHO}$, has $\text{C}$ bonded to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CH}_3$, H and $\text{CHO}$. That is four different groups, so it is chiral and exists as a pair of enantiomers.

Draw the mirror pair in 3D**
Put the chiral C in the centre. Draw one isomer, for example with $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ up, $\text{CHO}$ right, H on a dashed wedge and $\text{CH}_3$ on a solid wedge. For the second isomer, keep the same connectivity but swap any two groups in space, for example H and $\text{CHO}$, so the wedge and dash arrangement is mirrored. Check they are mirror images that cannot be superimposed.

Final answer: The chiral compound is Q, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CHO}$.
Draw the two enantiomers with central chiral C bonded to $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$, $\text{CH}_3$, H and CHO, with wedge and dash positions swapped to give non-superimposable mirror images.

hints: Recall which structural group gives a positive iodoform test with alkaline $\text{I}_2(\text{aq})$, the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ group or the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})$ group.
walkthrough:
Link the reagent to the functional group**
Alkaline $\text{I}_2$ is the iodoform test. Think of it as a detector for the $\text{CH}_3\text{C=O}$ fragment in a methyl ketone. Aldehydes P, Q, R, S cannot give it, and ketone U, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, has no $\text{COCH}_3$ group. Only T and V contain $\text{COCH}_3$, so only they give the yellow $\text{CHI}_3$ precipitate.

hints: Remember the characteristic colour and physical state of $\text{CHI}_3$ formed in a positive test.
Think about what happens to the $\text{COCH}_3$ group when it is cleaved, the $\text{CH}_3$ part becomes $\text{CHI}_3$ and the rest becomes a carboxylate that is protonated on acidification.
walkthrough:
State the visual positive result**
When the methyl ketone reacts, the $\text{COCH}_3$ methyl group is fully iodinated and then split off. The fragment $\text{CI}_3^-$ picks up a proton to give $\text{CHI}_3$, tri-iodomethane, which you see as a pale yellow solid precipitating from the colourless solution as the brown $\text{I}_2$ colour disappears.

Work out the paired organic product**
The rest of the molecule becomes a carboxylate salt, $\text{RCOO}^-$, under the alkaline conditions. Because the mixture is then acidified, you isolate the free carboxylic acid $\text{RCOOH}$. For T, $\text{R} = \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2$, so $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. For V, $\text{R} = \text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CH}$, so $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCOOH}$. Either pair with $\text{CHI}_3$ is correct.

Final answer: observation: yellow solid / yellow precipitate
two carbon-containing products: $\text{CHI}_3$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ (from T) OR $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCOOH}$ (from V)

hints: Look for a structure with only two proton environments where neither environment has protons on an adjacent carbon to cause splitting.
walkthrough:
Find two isolated proton sets**
A singlet means zero neighbouring protons (n+1 = 1). In S, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CCHO}$, the nine methyl protons are all equivalent and attached to a quaternary C with no protons, so they give one singlet. The aldehyde proton is attached to $\text{C=O}$ with no protons on the adjacent C, so it gives a second singlet. No other isomer has only two environments both without neighbours.

hints: Count the peaks in Fig. 7.1 and note the triplet around $\delta$ 1.1 and quartet around $\delta$ 2.4, then match to a highly symmetric ketone.
walkthrough:
Match symmetry to the simple spectrum**
Fig. 7.1 shows only two proton signals apart from TMS, a triplet near $\delta$ 1.1 and a quartet near $\delta$ 2.4. That fits $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ perfectly. The two $\text{CH}_3$ groups are equivalent and the two $\text{CH}_2$ groups are equivalent by symmetry, giving just two environments in a 3:2 ratio, with the tall triplet being the six $\text{CH}_3$ protons.

hints: Apply the n+1 rule to the $\text{CH}_3$ protons in U and count how many protons sit on the directly attached $\text{CH}_2$ group.
walkthrough:
Use n+1 to explain the triplet**
Focus on the $\text{CH}_3$ protons giving the $\delta$ 1.1 signal. Right next door is a $\text{CH}_2$ group with two equivalent protons. Using n+1 = 2+1 = 3, the signal is split into three lines, a triplet.

Final answer: name: triplet
reason: two hydrogen atoms / protons on neighbouring / adjacent carbon atom

hints: Recall the inert standard added to NMR samples that is defined as $\delta$ = 0 ppm.
walkthrough:
Name the zero reference**
All chemical shifts are measured relative to an internal standard that gives a single sharp peak well away from sample signals. That is tetramethylsilane, TMS, $\text{Si(CH}_3\text{)}_4$, set to $\delta$ = 0.

hints: Count distinct carbon environments in each structure, remembering that equivalent methyl groups in $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}$ or $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}$ give one signal.
Check U carefully for a plane of symmetry through the carbonyl group that makes the two ethyl groups identical.
walkthrough:
Count unique carbons for R and S**
For R, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{CHO}$, the two $\text{CH}_3$ carbons are equivalent, plus $\text{CH}$, plus $\text{CH}_2$, plus $\text{CHO}$ gives 4 peaks. For S, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CCHO}$, the three $\text{CH}_3$ carbons are equivalent, plus the quaternary $\text{C}$, plus $\text{CHO}$ gives 3 peaks.

Count unique carbons for T and U**
For T, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$, every carbon is in a different environment, so 5 peaks. For U, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, the molecule is symmetric about $\text{C=O}$: the two $\text{CH}_3$ carbons match and the two $\text{CH}_2$ carbons match, plus $\text{C=O}$ gives 3 peaks.
Final answer: R: 4, S: 3, T: 5, U: 3
